title: Choosing Native vs Cross-Platform
summary: The decision framework a team should actually reason through when choosing a mobile stack — engineering velocity versus platform fidelity, total cost of ownership, and the two ways teams get this decision wrong.

slides.markdown:
"Should we use Flutter, React Native, or go native?" is one of the most-asked mobile system design questions precisely because there's no universally correct answer — it's a genuine trade-off, and interviewers are testing whether you reason through it or just declare a favorite.

This topic builds the actual decision framework: the core trade-off (velocity vs fidelity), when each direction wins, total cost of ownership over the app's actual lifetime rather than just initial build cost, and how teams share business logic across native codebases without going fully cross-platform at all.

slides.subTitle: engineering velocity vs platform fidelity
slides.markdown:
Strip away framework marketing and the decision reduces to one axis: how much do you value **shipping one codebase faster** versus **matching each platform's native behavior and performance ceiling exactly**?

Cross-platform wins on velocity — one team, one codebase, one release cadence, faster iteration on product changes that ship simultaneously everywhere. Native wins on fidelity — no abstraction layer between your code and the platform, so you get every OS capability on day one, exactly the platform's real look-and-feel with zero adaptation work, and no framework-specific performance ceiling to hit.

Every other consideration in this topic — team structure, product category, growth stage — is really a way of answering 'which side of this trade-off actually matters more for this specific product, right now.'

slides.subTitle: heavy graphics, deep integration, camera/AR-first apps
slides.markdown:
Native is the stronger default when the product's core value proposition **is** platform-specific capability, not just UI. Concrete cases:

- **Camera/AR-first apps** — real-time video processing pipelines, ARKit/ARCore integration, and custom camera controls are exactly where cross-platform frameworks' abstraction layers cost the most and buy the least.
- **Heavy custom graphics or games** — a game engine (Unity, custom Metal/OpenGL rendering) already IS its own cross-platform strategy at a lower level; wrapping it in Flutter or React Native adds a layer with no benefit.
- **Deep OS integration** — apps built around widgets, App Clips, Live Activities, or Android-specific system integrations that need to be first-class, not bolted on via a plugin that may lag the OS release.
- **Performance-ceiling-sensitive apps** — anything where even a small, consistent overhead compounds, like a high-frequency trading or real-time collaboration app with strict latency budgets.

slides.subTitle: content-driven apps, small teams, fast iteration
slides.markdown:
Cross-platform is the stronger default when the product's value is mostly in **content, business logic, or speed of iteration**, not platform-specific capability:

- **Content-driven apps** — a news reader, an e-commerce catalog, a form-heavy internal tool. The UI is largely lists, cards, and forms — exactly what Flutter/React Native render well, with no deep platform integration needed.
- **Small teams / startups validating product-market fit** — one team shipping to both platforms simultaneously, with limited engineering headcount to split across two native codebases, matters more early on than squeezing out the last 10% of platform fidelity.
- **Apps needing frequent, simultaneous cross-platform releases** — a feature that must ship to iOS and Android the same week benefits enormously from one shared codebase and release process instead of coordinating two.
- **MVPs and apps expected to pivot** — cross-platform's velocity advantage compounds when the product itself is still changing shape.

slides.subTitle: two codebases vs one plus patches
slides.markdown:
| | Two native codebases | One cross-platform codebase |
|---|---|---|
| Initial build cost | higher (duplicate work) | lower |
| Ongoing feature velocity | slower (build twice) | faster (build once) |
| Platform-specific patch cost | none extra — it's native already | real but usually a minority of the codebase |
| Team structure needed | two specialized teams (iOS + Android) | one team, broader but shallower per-platform expertise |
| Long-term framework risk | none (platform vendors maintain the SDKs) | real — framework deprecation, breaking upgrades, third-party library abandonment |

The framework-risk row is the one teams most often skip: a cross-platform choice ties the app's future to a third party's roadmap and community health, not just Apple's/Google's. Evaluate a framework's maintenance trajectory (release cadence, breaking-change history, how actively core libraries are maintained) as part of total cost, not just today's feature set.

slides.subTitle: a shared core module
slides.markdown:
The framework choice isn't binary. A common, less-discussed middle path: keep **fully native UI** on both platforms, but share the **business logic** — networking, data models, validation rules, core algorithms — through a shared core module written in something like Kotlin Multiplatform (compiling to both a JVM library for Android and a native binary for iOS) or a Rust core with native bindings on each platform.

This captures a meaningful chunk of cross-platform's velocity win (the logic layer, often the most bug-prone and expensive-to-duplicate part) while keeping every pixel of UI genuinely native, with zero framework-imposed rendering ceiling. The cost is real too: the shared-core boundary itself needs careful API design and two native UI layers still need to be built and maintained — this isn't free, just a different point on the trade-off spectrum than either full native duplication or a full cross-platform UI framework.

A recurring team mistake: choosing a framework because it's trending, a senior engineer used it at a previous job, or a conference talk made it sound inevitable — without actually mapping the product's real requirements (does it need deep camera integration? is simultaneous release timing actually critical? how big is the team, and what's its existing skill set?) against the trade-off.

The fix is writing down the product's actual constraints *before* comparing frameworks: what does day-one need to do, what's the team's existing expertise (a team of five React engineers with zero Swift/Kotlin experience has a real, quantifiable cost to going fully native that a framework comparison chart doesn't capture), and what's the realistic 18-month roadmap. Decide from those constraints, then pick the framework that fits — not the reverse.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: the decision isn't permanent, but reversing it is expensive
slides.markdown:
A mid-level answer treats this as a one-time, static decision. A senior answer knows a few real companies have successfully migrated from cross-platform to native (or vice versa) as their product matured — but also knows that migration is genuinely expensive, usually multi-quarter, and rarely done incrementally without real product risk during the transition.

The practical framing worth stating in an interview: pick the option that's right for the **next 12–18 months** of the product's actual life cycle, not a permanent bet — but go in explicitly aware that reversing it later costs real engineering time, so the decision deserves the constraint-gathering rigor from the pitfall above, not a coin flip made because the deadline is tomorrow. For the concrete architectural patterns a mobile client actually needs once the stack is chosen — layering, offline-first design, sync — the Mobile System Design group's topics apply regardless of which stack won this decision.
